tool.name: KernelDensityGenerate
tool.summary: Creates a kernel-density surface from point features. The quartic kernel reproduces the Esri Kernel Density tool; other finite-support kernel shapes, an explicit planar/geodesic distance choice, and three output value types are also offered.
tool.usage:
A kernel density surface estimates the intensity of a point pattern: each input point is replaced by a smooth, finite-support kernel that adds weight to nearby cells out to the search radius (bandwidth) and drops to zero beyond it, and the overlapping kernels are summed. Such surfaces are widely used to estimate animal utilization distributions (home ranges) and the density of mapped features.
Kernel shape: seven finite-support kernels are offered, all of which reach zero at the search radius -- Quartic (the Esri Kernel Density method), Uniform, Triangular, Epanechnikov, Triweight, Tricube, and Cosine. The kernels differ in how sharply weight falls off with distance; all are normalized so that each point contributes the same total volume. Infinite-support kernels (such as the Gaussian), which never reach zero, are intentionally not offered.
Distance method: Planar measures straight-line distance in the projection's linear units; Geodesic measures true distance on the spheroid (Haversine). Input data in a geographic (latitude-longitude) coordinate system is always analyzed geodesically, and the distance method is then fixed to Geodesic.
Output cell values: Densities reports point density per a chosen area unit (the Esri behavior); Expected counts reports the expected number of points per cell (the cell values sum to the total number of input points); Proportion under the curve reports, for each cell, the cumulative proportion of the total volume under the surface, running from about 0 at the outer edge to 1 at the peak (oriented like the raw density). The proportion surface is intended to be contoured directly -- contour it at one minus the desired percentage to obtain home-range isopleths -- and is recognized as such by the Kernel Density Probability Contours tool.
Search radius (bandwidth): if you do not specify one, a default is computed by Silverman's rule of thumb (the same default the Esri tool uses), based only on the spatial distribution of the points. Treat the default as a starting guess and supply your own value when you have a better one.
Environments: this tool honors the Output Coordinate System, Cell Size, Processing Extent, Snap Raster, and Mask environments. If no Processing Extent is set, the output extent is the bounding rectangle of the input points expanded by the search radius, so the surface is not clipped at the points.
References: Silverman, B.W. (1986). Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis. Chapman and Hall, London. Worton, B.J. (1989). Kernel methods for estimating the utilization distribution in home-range studies. Ecology 70(1):164-168.

dialogReference.para: The point features whose density is estimated. If the layer has a selection, only the selected points are used. Input in a geographic coordinate system is analyzed with geodesic distances.
An optional numeric field giving each point a weight (for example, a count of animals or a magnitude). If left as NONE, every point is weighted as 1.
The output kernel density raster. A suggested name is filled in from the input feature class; change it as needed.

The cell size of the output raster, as a number or an existing raster. When you choose the input points, this is auto-filled using the same logic as the Esri tool: the Cell Size environment if set, otherwise the Snap Raster's cell size, otherwise the shorter side of the output extent divided by 250. Edit it to override.
The bandwidth: the distance at which each point's kernel falls to zero. Leave empty to compute a default by Silverman's rule of thumb (the same default the Esri Kernel Density tool uses):
Default = 0.9 * min( SD, sqrt(1 / ln(2)) * Dm ) * n^(-1/5)

where SD is the standard distance of the points about their mean center, Dm is the median distance from the points to the mean center, and n is the number of points (or the sum of the Population field). In effect it takes the smaller of the standard distance and the scaled median distance, then reduces that value - by a factor of 0.9 and by the number of points raised to the -1/5 power - so the bandwidth gets smaller as the number of points grows.
The default is only a best guess based on where the points lie relative to each other; specify your own radius whenever you have a more meaningful value.
The shape of the kernel placed over each point. All seven options have finite support (they reach zero at the search radius):

bulletList.bullet_item: Quartic (Esri KD method) - the biweight kernel used by the Esri Kernel Density tool; a smooth bell that reaches zero at the radius.
Uniform - a flat disk (every location within the radius gets equal weight).
Triangular - weight falls off linearly with distance.
Epanechnikov - a gentle parabola; statistically efficient.
Triweight - more sharply peaked than the quartic.
Tricube - a sharply peaked kernel common in local regression.
Cosine - a raised-cosine taper to zero.

dialogReference.para: Planar measures straight-line distance in the projection's linear units. Geodesic measures true distance on the spheroid (Haversine). Geographic (latitude-longitude) inputs are always geodesic, and this control is then locked to Geodesic.
Densities - point density per the chosen Area unit (the Esri behavior).
Expected counts - the expected number of points per cell; the cell values sum to the total number of input points.

Proportion under curve - the cumulative proportion of the total volume under the surface, from about 0 at the outer edge to 1 at the peak. Contour this surface at one minus a target percentage to obtain home-range isopleths; the Kernel Density Probability Contours tool recognizes this output automatically.
The area unit for the Densities output (for example, Square kilometers, Hectares, or Acres). Enabled only when Output cell values is Densities.

scriptExample.title: KernelDensityEnhanced example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Build a quartic kernel density surface (densities per square kilometer) from animal relocations, letting Silverman's rule choose the bandwidth.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.KernelDensityGenerate( in_features="Animal_Relocations", out_raster=r"C:\Project\HomeRange.gdb\KD_density", kernel="Quartic (Esri KD method)", distance_method="Planar", out_value="Densities", area_unit="Square kilometers")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Creates a kernel-density surface from points, with a choice of kernel shape, planar or geodesic distances, and density, expected-count, or proportion output.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Creates a kernel-density surface from point features. Each point is replaced by a finite-support kernel (quartic, uniform, triangular, Epanechnikov, triweight, tricube, or cosine) that contributes weight to cells within the search radius; overlapping kernels are summed. The quartic kernel reproduces the Esri Kernel Density tool. Distances may be planar or geodesic (geodesic is required for geographic data). Output cell values can be densities per a chosen area unit, expected point counts per cell, or a proportion-under-the-surface (volume) raster. If no search radius is given, a default is computed by Silverman's rule of thumb. The tool honors the Output Coordinate System, Cell Size, Processing Extent, Snap Raster, and Mask environments.
